blocks.text: In the dry months of harmattan, pull a wool jumper over your head in a dark room and you hear tiny cracks and see sparks. Touch a metal door handle after shuffling across a nylon rug and you get a sharp sting. Charge that built up on you has jumped the air gap — the same physics that lives in a gold-leaf electroscope and in every lightning flash.

blocks.markdown:
Electric charge comes in two kinds, **positive** and **negative**. **Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.** Charge is conserved: it is never created or destroyed, only separated or transferred. The SI unit is the **coulomb** (C).

A body can be charged in three ways:

- **Friction** — rubbing two insulators (a plastic biro on dry hair, a glass rod on silk) transfers electrons. The material that **gains** electrons becomes negative; the one that **loses** them becomes positive.
- **Contact** — a charged conductor touches an uncharged one and charge shares between them. Both end up with the **same** sign.
- **Induction** — a charged body is brought near, *not* touching. Charge in the conductor is redistributed. If the far side is then **earthed**, charge of one sign flows to earth; remove the earth and then the charged body, and the conductor is left with the **opposite** sign.

blocks.title: Earthing and the gold-leaf electroscope
blocks.text: Earthing means connecting a conductor to the earth so that charge can flow on or off until the conductor's potential is zero. On a gold-leaf electroscope the leaves diverge when the cap is charged (like charges on the rod and leaves repel). A like charge brought near increases the divergence; an unlike charge decreases it. Touching the cap with a finger earths it and the leaves collapse.

blocks.caption: Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges in air or vacuum

blocks.markdown:
**Coulomb's law** states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. The force is repulsive if the charges have the same sign and attractive if they have opposite signs. $k$ is Coulomb's constant. Work entirely in SI units: charges in coulombs, $r$ in metres, $F$ in newtons.

A useful conversion: $1\ \mu\text{C} = 1 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C}$.

blocks.title: Force between two point charges
blocks.prompt: Two point charges of $+2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ and $+3.0\ \mu\text{C}$ are 30 cm apart in air. Calculate the force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. Take $k = 9.0 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-2}$.

steps.text: Evaluate the numerator and the denominator.
State the force. Both charges are positive, so they repel.

blocks.markdown:
### Electric field intensity and electric potential

The **electric field intensity** $E$ at a point is the force experienced by a unit positive charge placed at that point:

$$E = \frac{F}{q} = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$$

Its SI unit is the **newton per coulomb** (N C⁻¹), which is the same as the **volt per metre** (V m⁻¹). The direction of $E$ is the direction a positive test charge would move — away from a positive source charge, towards a negative one.

The **electric potential** $V$ at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point:

$$V = \frac{kQ}{r}$$

Its SI unit is the **volt** (V), equal to one joule per coulomb. Potential is a scalar; field intensity is a vector.

blocks.caption: Force and field both fall as 1/r²; potential falls only as 1/r.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Convert µC to C (× 10⁻⁶) and cm to m before substituting. If a question doubles the separation, F and E each become one-quarter; V becomes one-half. Never treat potential as a vector — you add potentials algebraically, including the sign of each charge.

points: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is conserved and is measured in coulombs.
A body can be charged by friction, by contact (same sign is shared) or by induction (the remaining charge has the opposite sign). Earthing lets charge flow to or from the earth.
A gold-leaf electroscope detects charge: the leaves diverge, and a like charge increases the divergence.
Coulomb's law: F = k q₁ q₂ / r² with k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Use SI units.
Electric field intensity E = F/q = kQ/r² (vector, unit N C⁻¹). Electric potential V = kQ/r (scalar, unit V).
